title: TCP: Summarize the completeness bitmask as a string
description:
Similarly to the TCP Flags summary, a Completeness summary is
added then filtering is made easier. This field is called
'tcp.completeness.str'

file for testing :
[completeness-variations.pcapng](/uploads/c54818390e6b8446be246ead92a51c8c/completeness-variations.pcapng)

See #18911

notes.body: mentioned in issue #18911

If you're worried about the performance hit from calculating the string, there's two options. You could call:

`if (proto_field_is_referenced(field_tree, hf_tcp_completeness_str))`

and only generate the string and add it if that is true (either a visible tree, or filtering that field). I haven't made extensive use of that myself.

The other option, as you note, is to add the string as conversation data to the tcp conversation, by adding a field to the `struct tcp_analysis` and updating it whenever you update the conversation completeness.

A single initial for "SYN-ACK" is tricky to decide upon, unlike with the SYN and ACK packets. It ends up looking the same as SYN packet. (It also ends up looking like an unfortunate acronym, oh well.)

Thanks for the suggestions. I kept the additional conversation string idea to track the human-readable value.
I re-ordered your _bitfield waterfall_ the other way around then it is consistent with what is done with the `TCP Flags` (the smallest bit at the bottom).
If the acronym is uncomfortable to anyone, maybe opt for T instead of S for interpreting SYN-ACK, but that will turn filter building less intuitive.

This needs to be `wmem_file_scope()` instead of `pinfo->pool`. `tcpd` is created at file scope, because it persists for the lifetime of the capture file. `pinfo->pool` is freed when the packet is finished dissecting.

If you do create it at `wmem_file_scope()`, you don't need to call `g_strdup()`, and you don't have to worry about it leaking. (As it is now, it leaks because you don't free the string each time it changes.)
You could still choose to free the string when it changes, although each conversation is limited in how many times it can change so that's not necessary.

@@ -720,6 +720,11 @@ data transfer will be found with a longer filter as closing a connection can be
 associated with FIN or RST packets, or even both :
 'tcp.completeness==31 or tcp.completeness==47 or tcp.completeness==63'
 
+Another way to select specific conversation values is to filter on the
+tcp.completeness.str field. Thus, 'tcp.completeness.str matches "(R.*|F)[^D]ASS"'
+will find all 'Complete, NO_DATA' conversations, while the 'Complete, WITH_DATA'
+ones will be found with 'tcp.completeness.str matches "(R.*|F)DASS"'.
